code-is-easy-people-are-hard.core: Beyond a certain level, technical skill is table stakes. Impact depends on influence, collaboration, conflict handling and communication. Behavioural interviews probe these through past stories, because past behaviour is the best available predictor of future behaviour.

first_principles.problem: A strong coder is rejected at senior level because their stories show no influence beyond their own tickets.
truths: Large systems are built by groups.
Misalignment wastes more time than bad code.
Interviewers infer future behaviour from past stories.
derivation: Prepare **8–10 stories** covering conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity and impact.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor
analogy.story: Every musician can play; the conductor's value is getting them to play together.
analogy.breaks: Conductors have formal authority; engineers often lead without it.

example.title: A STAR story
flow: S: on-call had 40 pages/week
T: I owned reducing toil
A: I ran an alert audit and led 3 teams' fixes
R: 8 pages/week; adopted org-wide

check.q: Why do behavioural interviews ask about past situations?
check.a: Past behaviour in real situations is a better predictor than hypothetical answers.

leading-without-authority.core: Senior engineers drive change across teams they don't manage, using influence: a clear problem statement backed by data, shared goals, early involvement of stakeholders, small proofs of concept and credit given generously. Trust is the currency.

first_principles.problem: You need five teams to adopt a new deployment standard, and none report to you.
truths: People support what they help create.
derivation: **Show data** and a proof of concept.

analogy.title: A gardener versus a mechanic
analogy.story: You can't bolt plants together; you create conditions where they grow.
analogy.breaks: Gardens grow without persuasion; people need to see what's in it for them.

example.title: Rolling out a CI standard
flow: Data: build failures cost 300 h/month
Pilot with one willing team → 40% faster
Pilot team presents results
4 more teams opt in

points: Make it easy and share credit.

check.q: Why let a pilot team present the results?
check.a: Peers' endorsement is more persuasive than the proposer's, and it shares ownership.

conflict-resolution-the-sbi-model.core: SBI feedback (Situation, Behaviour, Impact) keeps hard conversations factual: describe when and where, the observable behaviour (not personality) and its impact, then invite their perspective. It reduces defensiveness and focuses on solutions.

first_principles.problem: 'You're always dismissive in reviews' starts an argument instead of a change.
truths: Observable facts are hard to dispute.
derivation: **Impact**: 'she stopped contributing, and we missed her concern.'
**Ask**: 'What was going on from your side?'

analogy.title: A referee citing a specific foul
analogy.story: 'Handball at 23 minutes' is accepted; 'you're a dirty player' starts a fight.
analogy.breaks: Referees decide alone; SBI invites dialogue and the other person's context.

example.title: Code review conflict
flow: S: 'On the payments PR yesterday…'
B: '…the comment said this is junior code'
I: 'the author felt discouraged and paused the work'
Ask: 'How did you intend it?'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A calm conversation and a change in review tone.

check.q: Why focus on behaviour rather than personality?
check.a: Behaviour is observable and changeable; personality labels feel like attacks and provoke defensiveness.

the-interview-tell-me-about-a-time-you-d.core: This question tests whether you can disagree constructively and then commit. A strong answer shows you raised concerns with data through the right channels, understood leadership's context, proposed alternatives or mitigations, and either changed the decision or committed fully once it was made.

first_principles.problem: Candidates either tell a story where they caved silently or where they fought until they 'won'.
truths: Leaders have context you may lack.
derivation: Describe **disagree and commit** or a changed decision.

analogy.title: A ship's navigator warning the captain
analogy.story: The navigator presents the charts clearly; once the captain decides, the navigator helps execute safely.
analogy.breaks: Ships have strict hierarchy; good orgs genuinely change course on strong evidence.

example.title: Launch date disagreement
flow: Leadership set a launch two weeks early
I showed load-test data: 30% failure at peak
Proposed phased launch at 10% traffic
Accepted; phase 1 found a bug; full launch on time

check.a: Voice disagreement openly, but once the decision is made, support it fully rather than undermining it.

sponsoring-vs-mentoring.core: Mentoring is advice: talking with someone about how to grow. Sponsoring is advocacy: using your own credibility to put someone forward for stretch projects, promotions and visibility when they're not in the room. Staff+ engineers are expected to do both, and sponsorship moves careers more.

first_principles.problem: A talented engineer gets great advice for years but is never considered for high-visibility work.
truths: Opportunities are allocated in rooms you're not in.
Underrepresented engineers are often over-mentored and under-sponsored.
derivation: **Set them up to succeed** with support.

analogy.title: A coach versus an agent
analogy.story: A coach improves your game; an agent gets you onto the team.
analogy.breaks: Agents take a commission; sponsors risk their reputation instead.

example.title: Sponsoring a mid-level engineer
flow: Recommend her to lead the cache migration
Pair on the design doc review
Credit her in the all-hands demo
Cite the project in calibration

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Promotion case built on visible work.

check.q: What's the key difference between mentoring and sponsoring?
check.a: Mentors give advice; sponsors actively advocate and create opportunities using their own credibility.
